content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method that combines self-supervised monocular depth estimation and multiplane nerf rendering. Therefore, the proposed method can jointly learn depth, pose and rendering from video without ground-truth annotations. The idea is interesting, however, the proposed method lacks technical novelty. More importantly, there are many unfair settings and unclear details in experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

The idea of combining self-supervised depth estimation and nerf-based rendering is interesting.

Weakness

1. The technical novelty is limited. The proposed method is just a simple combination of existing self-supervised monocular depth estimation and multiplane nerf rendering methods. The authors argue that “auto scale calibration” is one key technical contribution, but it indeed consists of “depth L1 loss” and “photometric loss”, which have been already widely-used in supervised/self-supervised depth estimation methods.

2. As discussed in [a], many existing self-supervised depth estimation methods often fail to provide reasonable results in indoor scenes. Also, as reported in [b], monodepth2 sometimes fails to converge when training in indoor scenes due to complex camera motion. I suspect that the “monodepth2*” shown in Table 2 is exactly such a failure model. Could the authors show the visual results? If so, multiple runs of training are required, and the results of correctly trained models should be reported.

3. In Table 1, is monodepth2 trained on ScanNet?

4. As mentioned in W2, monodepth2 is not  a good baseline for comparing depth estimation results in indoor scenes. Alternatively, [a, b, c] and P2Net [Yu et al., 2020] should be compared. The code of [a, c] is unavailable, but the results could be pasted from their papers. The code of [b] and P2Net are publicly available, so the authors could train them using the same setting on the same dataset for fair comparison. 

5. I find that the authors have compared with P2Net in Table 3 for camera pose evaluation, why not compare with it  in Table 1 and Table 2 for depth estimation evaluation?

6. In Table 2, the comparison to KITTI-trained monodepth2 and manydepth on the NYUv2 dataset is unmeaningful. There is a significant domain gap between two datasets, and as I know, any method that is trained only on KITTI cannot show good results on NYUv2. Moreover, is the “monodepth2*” trained correctly in RealEstate here? Could the authors show the visual results?

7. In Table 3, is SfMLearner trained on KITTI? Is P2Net trained on NYUv2? As I know, the CNN-based depth estimation could generalize well on similar scenes, while the relative pose estimation is often not generalized well. Could the authors train P2Net or [b] in the same dataset for camera pose comparison?

8. There is no qualitative depth estimation comparison with other methods.



Reference
[a] Moving Indoor: Unsupervised Video Depth Learning in Challenging Environments, ICCV 2019
[b] Auto-Rectify Network for Unsupervised Indoor Depth Estimation, TPAMI 2021
[c] MonoIndoor: Towards Good Practice of Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation for Indoor Environments, ICCV 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Limited technical novelty. Many details are unclear.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I recommend rejection because 
(1) the comparison is unfair 
(2) many experiment details are unclear
(3) highly related methods are not compared
(4) novelty is limited

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an autoencoder architecture that estimates 6-DoF camera motion and a depth map from a video image sequence. The authors employ the multiplane NeRF technique as the decoder to represent the 3D scene and propose an auto-scale calibration approach for the estimated camera pose and the disparity map. They evaluate the proposed method on three different tasks: monocular depth estimation, camera pose estimation, and single novel view synthesis compared to the SOTA methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
o Strength
- Related papers and work are well-investigated and well-written.
- Auto-scale calibration looks like an interesting approach to solving the scale issue in the monocular camera settings.
- The proposed network (Figure 2) is a good combination of existing methods (MINE and Multiplane NeRF) with the proposed auto-scale calibration.

o Weakness
- There is no experimental result of camera pose estimation for other famous, de-facto datasets such as KITTI, TUM, ICL-NUIM, and EuRoC datasets to evaluate the proposed learning approach.
- Further performance comparisons with classical VO/SLAM methods and SOTA approaches (ex. ORB-SLAM3, DROID-SLAM) are needed in the camera pose evaluation part.
- Although the authors emphasize that the proposed method operates on large-scale videos in the paper, the actual test environments are not large-scale at all. The length of the camera trajectory is at most ~ 1 m.
- Compared algorithms including MonodepthV2 are old-fashioned, which is proposed in 2019. The authors need to evaluate the proposed method with some SOTA approaches.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed method in this paper is a good combination of existing approaches with incremental (minor) new contributions, and auto-scale calibration. The clarity and quality of this paper are not bad, but I am not sure whether there is a novelty to get accepted for ICLR.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed approach is an interesting idea, but lacks sufficient experimental results. See the comments above for more details.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper propose an unsupervised depth estimation strategy by adding a multiplane image representation [zhou et.al 2018] and nerf rendering process in view sysnthesis. [Multiplane Nerf] as presented in the paper. 

The architecture combined with the proposed losses produces SoTA performance [in depth estimation, camera pose estimation & view systhesis] in several indoor open benchmarks such as ScanNet & NYU v2.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros: 

1) The architecture presented sounds in terms of the presentation since multiplane nerf produces better supervision than a vanila warping as induced in methods such as [MonoDepthv2 etc.]. 

2) The paper did extensive comparison with and good reference to other related works. On all three tasks the results out-performs the counter parts with a significant margin. 

Cons:
Since the Multiplane Nerf is introduced in [MINE] Li et.al 2021. In my perspective, this paper is majorly apply similar architecture for the task of unsupervised depth estimation with a new proposed camera encoder and a modified . In addition, in their paper, they already show a good depth estimation results with pose from SfM using COLMAP. So the novelty of this paper is comparably limited. 

From the experiments, I originally thought by using learnt pose, the results could be comparable with MINE with their learnt camera pose, but from Tab.2 & Tab.3, it seems the learnt camera pose encoder performs much worse [depth 0.11 vs 0.17] [PSNR 28.39 vs 26.68] 

Other questions:

Why use MnasNet/Res50 for depth encoder but not transformer based architectures such as DPT [Vision Transformers for Dense Prediction]?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1) The paper presents clearly and the conclusion sounds in my perspective. 
2) Novelty is somehow limited as presented previously.  Another novelty the author mentioned is caliberation loss which is a simple L1 loss by comparing the depth better Depth decoder and Nerf rendering, which is ablated in Tab.5 [while not abalated in depth&pose accuracy]. In my opinion, it might not be strong enough in claiming a major contribution for the community. 
3) The paper should be easy to reproduce by following the open-source of MINE
content.summary_of_the_review:
In summy, the paper provides a good representation for unsupervised depth&camera pose estimation by applying Multiplane Nerf [Li et.al 2021], which shows promising results in multiple tasks. 
But the novelty is limited in terms of technique contribution.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper combined self-supervised learning based depth and pose estimation task and a multiplane nerf approach together.
Also, they propose a scale calibration method to align rendered depth, prediction depth, and relative pose by utilizing depth consistency and image projection loss.
However, the proposed depth consistency and projection lossse are quite common and widely utilized in the self-supervised learning field.
I think this paper has a contribution in terms of proposing a direction of combining self-supervised depth/pose/Nerf. But, the novelty is generally weak and needs to improve.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strength]
+ combine self-supervised depth and pose estimation task and multiple Nerf approach.
+ shows better performance in various benchmark

[Weakness]
- The novelty of scale calibration is weak. Image reconstruction loss and depth consistency loss are well-known and obvious solutions. 
- The novelty of multiplane Nerf of this paper. Multi-plane Nerf has already been proposed in various papers, I cannot find any improvement or difference in the proposed multiplane Nerf.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
[Clarity, Quality, Novelty, and Reproducibility]
- This paper needs to clarify their main contribution, novelty, and idea more clearly.
- The novelty of the proposed multi-plane Nerf, scale calibration is insufficient.
+ Author promises to open the source code publicly available.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Based on the strengths, weaknesses, and novelty, this paper needs to improve its contribution, novelty, and writing.
However, this paper has a contribution in terms of a solution for a combination of self-supervised depth, pose, and nerf tasks.  
But, currently, I am not absolutely sure of my decision. After checking the author's response and other reviewers' opinions, I have a chance to adjust my decision
